title: Perf vs Quality Guardrails (Q1 2026 perf baseline) — minimal spot-check plan
content:
Owner: Jonas Weber (Perf/Evals)
Reviewers: Dr. Maya Srinivasan (Applied ML), Claire Dubois (Methodology), Mateo Alvarez (Runtime)
Last updated: 2026-01-22

Context
This memo defines the minimum set of quality guardrails we will run alongside the Q1 2026 “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” project. The intent is not to build a full eval suite; it is to prevent performance work (kernels/scheduling/caching/quantization/instrumentation) from unintentionally changing decoding behavior or output quality while we establish the baseline numbers.

Non-goals
- We are not attempting to rank models or publish quality benchmarks.
- We are not attempting to provide broad safety evaluations.
- We are not attempting to cover every customer prompt shape.

Why this matters (failure modes we’ve seen or expect)
Performance changes can affect outputs via:
1) Decoding boundary changes (streaming chunks / tokenization boundaries)
   - “TTFT improved” by changing what counts as first token on wire, or emitting partial UTF-8 / partial JSON fragments.
   - Streaming cadence changes that alter client-side parsing for function calling.

2) Sampling changes (direct or accidental)
   - Temperature/top_p/top_k defaults drift; “seed” not honored.
   - Floating-point differences from kernel changes or mixed precision create output drift (esp. near decision boundaries).

3) Cache / KV reuse behavior
   - Incorrect KV cache reuse leads to semantically wrong continuation.
   - Prefix caching enabled/disabled changes effective prompt for some request paths.

4) Quantization and kernel fallbacks
   - Auto-selection fallback to a different kernel/precision path changes logits.
   - Different math modes (FP8/FP16/BF16) change output distributions.

5) Tokenizer / chat template drift
   - Model catalog updates or runtime upgrades inadvertently change chat templates.

6) Tool/function calling formatting
   - JSON schema adherence changes (extra fields, wrong types, trailing commas).

Principles
- Determinism where possible: for a small “must-not-break” set, require identical outputs under greedy decoding.
- Structural validity over subjective “quality”: for tool calls / structured output, prioritize parse rate and schema validity.
- Minimal but representative coverage: align to workload suite cohorts (chat streaming, long prefill summarization, tool calling, embeddings sanity).
- Reproducibility: spot-check results must tie back to the run manifest (ADR-0172) and be rerunnable.

Quality guardrails: what we will enforce for Q1 2026 baseline

A) Environment + configuration pinning (required for baseline runs)
For any run used to set or compare against the Q1 2026 baseline, the following must be captured and pinned in the run manifest:
- Model identifier + exact revision/hash (catalog version) + tokenizer version
- Chat template / system prompt template version (if applicable)
- Decoding configuration:
  - Greedy vs sampling mode
  - temperature, top_p, top_k, repetition penalty, frequency/presence penalties
  - seed handling semantics (server-side seed, per-request seed)
  - max_tokens, stop sequences
- Precision / quantization mode (and whether auto-selected)
- Kernel selection overrides (if any) and fallback reasons (see runtime kernel dump work)
- Caching mode (report both cold and warm scenarios; see caching decision thread)

Note: We do not require identical outputs between cold vs warm; we require that “warm” does not change semantics (no KV reuse correctness bugs). The checks below are designed to catch obvious cache correctness issues.

B) Minimal quality spot-check suite (required for baseline freeze; recommended for perf-canary)
We define a small suite of prompts (synthetic and/or redacted) with expected output constraints. This suite is intentionally small to keep runtime/cost low.

Suite overview (v1)
- Total prompts: 36 (target runtime < 8 minutes per model on benchmark fleet; can be sharded)
- Two modes:
  1) Deterministic greedy checks (exact match or exact structural checks)
  2) Sampling checks (non-exact; validate invariants and distribution sanity)

Workload mapping
1) Chat streaming (short prompts, variable decode)
2) Long-context summarization (large prefill, modest decode)
3) Tool/function calling (bursty multi-turn, strict JSON)
4) Embeddings (sanity checks on similarity ordering; not full retrieval eval)


B1) Deterministic greedy checks (must pass)
Run config:
- temperature=0
- top_p=1
- top_k=0 (or disabled)
- seed fixed where relevant (seed should be ignored for greedy, but still recorded)
- max_tokens set per prompt

Pass criteria:
- For text-only prompts: byte-for-byte exact match against the baseline anchor build output (after normalization rules below).
- For tool/function calling: JSON must parse; must conform to schema; canonicalized JSON must match baseline.

Normalization rules (to avoid false positives)
- Normalize line endings (CRLF vs LF)
- Trim trailing whitespace
- For JSON: parse and re-serialize with canonical ordering (stable key ordering) before compare
- Do NOT normalize Unicode beyond standard UTF-8 decode; we want to catch partial/invalid streaming fragments.

Greedy prompt list (high-level; exact texts stored in eval-harness prompt pack)
1) Chat/assistant: short instruction with one-sentence answer
2) Chat/assistant: math word problem with exact numeric final answer
3) Chat/assistant: “write a 5-bullet list with strict formatting”
4) Chat streaming: prompt designed to produce >150 tokens to exercise streaming chunking
5) Tool call: “extract fields into JSON with schema {name:string, amount:number, currency:string}”
6) Tool call: “choose one of N tools based on user query” (validate tool_name exactly)
7) Long prefill: summarization of synthetic doc (~12k tokens) with required headings
8) Long prefill: “find 3 specific facts” where the facts are present verbatim in the synthetic doc
9) KV/cache correctness probe: multi-turn chat where turn 2 depends on turn 1 exactly (detect missing/incorrect cache reuse)
10) “Stop sequence” test: response must stop before a sentinel token

Note to self / open question: we should ensure at least one prompt hits the known kernel selection boundary (sequence length regime where fallback risk is highest). Hiro/Yuki to suggest a regime-triggering prompt length.


B2) Sampling checks (should pass; non-blocking during early rollout, blocking at baseline freeze)
Run config:
- temperature=0.7
- top_p=0.95
- seed fixed per prompt
- generate N=3 samples per prompt (N small to keep cost down)

What we check:
1) Seed determinism: with fixed seed, repeated runs on same build should match exactly (or match within defined tolerance if we find GPU nondeterminism; goal is exact).
2) Basic output sanity:
   - Output is non-empty
   - No invalid UTF-8
   - No tool call JSON parse failures when tool mode is requested
3) Lightweight semantic invariants:
   - For “extract X/Y/Z” prompts: required fields present
   - For “choose tool” prompts: tool_name is one of allowed options

We explicitly do not attempt to measure “better/worse” for sampling outputs; we only attempt to catch major behavior drift (formatting, determinism, tool-call breakage).


C) Embeddings sanity checks (recommended; minimal)
Even though the perf suite includes an embeddings workload, quality checks are intentionally light:
- Use a small set of 24 synthetic sentence pairs (12 similar, 12 dissimilar)
- Compute cosine similarities and validate ranking:
  - Similar pairs should score higher than dissimilar pairs in at least 10/12 cases
- Track drift relative to baseline anchor:
  - If average cosine similarity on the “similar” set drops > 0.05, flag for review

Rationale: This is not a retrieval eval; it is a guardrail against wrong model revisions, tokenizer mismatches, or output corruption.


D) When to run what (gating policy for Q1 2026)
1) Baseline freeze (required)
- For each baseline anchor build (the runtime tag we declare as Q1 2026 baseline) and each top model family in scope:
  - Run B1 (greedy) + B2 (sampling) + embeddings sanity (C)
  - Store artifacts linked to run manifest id

2) Perf-canary nightly (recommended)
- Run B1 greedy subset (10 prompts) for 2–3 representative models (one per family) on at least us-east H100, plus one non-H100 SKU if scheduled.
- Run tool-call JSON validity prompts every night (these catch real breakages quickly).

3) PR gating (optional, limited)
- For changes touching decoding, chat templates, sampling, kernel selection, precision modes, or caching correctness:
  - Run B1 subset in CI (smaller set; <3 minutes)
- For pure scheduling/queueing instrumentation changes:
  - No PR gating by default; rely on nightly + release gating.

Proposed thresholds for “block” vs “warn”
- Block immediately:
  - Any greedy exact-match failure
  - Any tool-call JSON parse/schema failure
  - Any invalid UTF-8 / streaming corruption
- Warn (triage within 1 business day):
  - Sampling seed determinism failure (if confirmed nondeterminism isn’t expected)
  - Embeddings ranking check below threshold

Escalation path
- First responder: perf-canary triage channel + runtime oncall (if canary is paging)
- Owners:
  - Output drift / decoding params: Applied ML (Jonas), Runtime architecture (Noah)
  - Tool/function calling formatting: Applied ML + API/Console as needed
  - Kernel/precision path: Hiro/Yuki
  - Cache correctness: Omar


E) Prompt sourcing + privacy constraints
- Prompts in this spot-check suite are either:
  1) Fully synthetic, authored by Applied ML, or
  2) Derived from production telemetry cohorts but rewritten/redacted to remove any customer-identifying content.
- We will not store raw customer prompts in this suite.
- See ADR-0173 for the telemetry-to-workload derivation approach and privacy constraints.

Storage location and access
- Prompt packs live in eval-harness (internal) under a versioned directory (e.g., prompt_packs/perf_quality_guardrails/q1_2026_v1/).
- Baseline expected outputs are stored per model+revision+decode config with checksums.


F) Practical guidance (how to use this during baseline work)
If you are running a baseline sweep and you see a perf delta:
1) Confirm run manifests match (model revision, decoding, precision, caching mode).
2) Run the minimal spot-check suite on both builds (baseline anchor vs candidate) with greedy config.
3) If greedy outputs differ:
   - Check kernel selection dump and precision path
   - Check tokenizer/chat template versions
   - Check whether any “perf improvement” was achieved via changing streaming boundaries
4) If greedy matches but sampling differs:
   - Confirm seed semantics and determinism; check for nondeterministic kernels
   - Evaluate whether sampling drift is acceptable for this change (Applied ML sign-off required before baseline freeze)


Open questions / TODOs
- Define the final “baseline anchor build” identifier to pin expected outputs against (waiting on runtime tag confirmation thread).
- Confirm whether any current kernels are nondeterministic under our target CUDA/driver stack; if yes, document exceptions and adjust sampling checks.
- Add one prompt that explicitly stresses long-prefill + tool call in a single session (multi-turn with a tool call on turn 3) to better mirror production agentic patterns.
- Decide whether we want to record per-token logprobs for a tiny subset (2 prompts) as a deeper debugging artifact (not gating).

Appendix A: References
- ADR-0172: canonical metrics + run manifest format (tie spot-check outputs to manifest)
- ADR-0173: workload suite sourcing from prod telemetry (privacy + representativeness)
- eval-harness PR: lightweight quality spot-check hooks (PR-21590)

- perf_quality_guardrails.q1_2026_v1.greedy.core
- perf_quality_guardrails.q1_2026_v1.sampling.core
